newsitem.title: USA: Shots, floods, exploding hotel usher in US New Year.
newsitem.headline: Shots, floods, exploding hotel usher in US New Year.

text.p: Americans welcomed 1997 on Wednesday with traditional parades and football games but in the gambling capital of Las Vegas the new year came in with a bang -- literally.

Not to be outdone by the street party featuring half a million revellers in New York's Times Square, the celebration in the Nevada desert city climaxed with the 40-year-old Hacienda Hotel being demolished in a spectacular explosion.

After a six-minute fireworks display involving more than 3,000 aerial shells, the entire 600-foot (183-metre) facade of the Hacienda, wired with 750 detonations, erupted in computer-controled explosions to the delight of the crowd.
The building collapsed into a pile of rubble and in the tradition of America's home of excess, will be replaced by an even bigger hotel.
New Year celebrations were not so joyous, however, in the Pacific Northwest where a new storm caused mudslides and power outages in Washington state and flooding in California's wine country.
The latest in a series of punishing Pacific storms in the region since last week brought heavy rain and high winds, putting a damper on New Year's celebrations.
At least 11 deaths were blamed on the storms and property damage in Washington, Oregon and northern California was estimated at up to $250 million.
Torrential rain fell over northern California and the National Weather Service predicted "disastrous" flood levels for the Russian and Napa rivers in the wine country north of San Francisco.
Police all over the country meanwhile tried to discourage the tradition among some people of shooting off guns to welcome in the New Year.
There was tragedy in Houston, where a 7-year-old girl was killed by her father, when he tried to clear a jammed gun and fired it by accident.
A 39-year-old man in the Texas city was also accidentally killed when party-goers went outside to shoot their guns off at midnight.

In San Diego, California, near the Mexican border, police received 296 reports of shots being fired in the air. A spokesman said five men had been caught in the act and charged with reckless discharge of a weapon.

There was a shot fired near the route of the traditional Tournament of Roses Parade in Pasadena, just north of Los Angeles. A spokesman said an officer fired one round while arresting a man who tried to take his gun during a fracas in the early hours of Wednesday.

Rain was forecast to spoil the parade for the first time in 42 years, but it went off without a hitch under balmy weather. The weather was expected to hold for the traditional Rose Bowl college football game -- this year pitting Ohio State against Arizona State.

Los Angeles police made six drug arrests when more than 30 fans became ill at a rock concert. Police said four people were in critical condition after taking the drug Ecstasy, which had been handed out at the show by Seventh Heaven.
President Bill Clinton, his wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea left for the Caribbean to spend the rest of the week on the island of St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The president rang in the New Year early on Wednesday by singing songs around the piano at a gala that included 1,600 guests in Hilton Head, South Carolina.

New York meanwhile became "the brightest point on Earth" on the stroke of midnight as a half million merrymakers, exuberant and remarkably well-behaved, ushered in 1997 with the traditional ball drop in Times Square.

Lasers, strobes and other lights amounted to some 2 billion candlepower, said Gretchen Dykstra, president of the Times Square Business Improvement District. It made America's biggest city the "brightest point on Earth," she said.
The drop of the brightly lit rhinestone-decorated ball, an 89-year-old tradition, was accompanied by 3,000 pounds (1,300 kilograms) of confetti and 20,000 pompoms and balloons.
